anchor_text: Open your ears; for which of you will stop
summary: The play opens not with a named character but with an allegorical figure, Rumour, who enters 'painted full of tongues' — wearing a costume covered in fabric tongues, a visual emblem of false report. This induction (prologue spoken by a personified abstraction) tells the audience that everything they are about to hear from the rebel camp will be wrong.
detail: Allegorical figures wearing emblematic costumes were a familiar device from Tudor court masques and morality plays. The 'painted' costume of tongues signals at once that this is not a realistic character but a living symbol. Rumour then delivers the false report — that Hotspur won at Shrewsbury — that the entire first scene will track and correct. The device announces the play's central preoccupation: the gap between report and truth.

sources.name: Virgil / Ovid
sources.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 4.173-188 (Fama, the swift monster of tongues and ears); Ovid, Metamorphoses 12.39-63 (the House of Rumour).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1
Virgil Aeneid 4.173-188 (Fama with tongues/ears/eyes) and Ovid Metamorphoses 12.39-63 (House of Rumour) are both confirmed real passages at those line numbers.

The identification of Rumour's costume as a morality-play emblem and the description of the Induction's function as a device to prime the audience for the false-report plot are mainstream and well-supported.

anchor_text: from the orient to the drooping west, Making the wind my post-horse
summary: 'Orient' means the east (from Latin oriens, the rising sun); 'drooping west' is the west where the sun sets and sinks. A 'post-horse' was a horse kept at relay stations ('posts') along main roads so that royal messengers could ride at speed, swapping tired animals for fresh ones. Rumour claims to travel the whole world, from east to west, using the wind itself as its fast relay-horse.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'post-horse' n.: 'A horse kept at a post-station for the use of travelers posting; a horse used to ride post.' OED s.v. 'orient' adj. 1: 'Of or belonging to the east; eastern.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3
OED senses for 'post-horse' and 'orient' are standard, uncontroversial lexicographic references that support the claims made.
The glosses on 'orient' (east), 'drooping west' (the setting sun), and 'post-horse' (relay-horse at a posting station) are all standard, uncontroversial Elizabethan usage.

anchor_text: Rumour is a pipe Blown by surmises, jealousies, conjectures, And of so easy and so plain a stop
summary: Rumour compares itself to a musical pipe (a wind instrument like a recorder or flute). 'Surmises' are guesses; 'jealousies' means suspicious fears, not romantic jealousy; 'conjectures' are unsupported conclusions. A 'stop' is a finger-hole on a pipe — to cover a hole changes the note. Rumour says it is so simple that even the brainless mob can play it.
detail: The pipe metaphor is extended carefully: the pipe is 'blown' (it runs on breath and rumor, like all wind-instruments and all gossip), its 'stops' are easy enough for a fool to play. The same image of effortless manipulation governs Hamlet's famous anger at Guildenstern trying to 'play upon' him like a pipe (Hamlet 3.2). 'Jealousies' in the sense of suspicious fears is standard Elizabethan usage (OED s.v. 'jealousy' 2).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'stop' n.1, sense 20: 'A device in a wind instrument to alter the pitch of the note.' OED s.v. 'jealousy' 2: 'Suspicion; apprehension of evil; anxiety.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 15
OED s.v. 'stop' (wind-instrument finger-hole) and 'jealousy' sense 2 (suspicious fear) are real and support the glosses; the Hamlet 3.2 parallel is a correct cross-reference.

Reading 'stop' as a finger-hole, 'jealousies' as suspicious fears, and 'blown' as playing a wind instrument are all standard glosses; the Hamlet 3.2 parallel is apt and well-known, though the annotation is careful not to overstate it as a direct echo.

anchor_text: the blunt monster with uncounted heads, The still-discordant wavering multitude
summary: The 'blunt monster with uncounted heads' is the common people — the mob. 'Blunt' means dull-witted; 'uncounted' means too many to number. The image of the many-headed monster was a standard Elizabethan way of dismissing popular opinion as mindless and contradictory. Shakespeare uses the same image of the mob in Coriolanus.
detail: The contempt for the 'multitude' as a beast with too many heads to direct was a commonplace of conservative Elizabethan political thought; the official Homily Against Disobedience preached that the many could not rule themselves. 'Still-discordant' means always inconsistent, always out of tune with each other — fitting the pipe metaphor that precedes it.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'blunt': 'Dull in understanding.' OED s.v. 'still' adv. 2: 'Always, ever, constantly.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 18
Onions s.v. 'blunt' and OED s.v. 'still' adv. 2 are standard references that support the claimed senses; the Homily Against Disobedience contextual claim is accurate.

The many-headed-monster image for the mob is a documented Elizabethan commonplace (Coriolanus, Sidney's Defence, official homilies), and 'blunt' as dull-witted and 'still' as always are standard glosses.

anchor_text: My well-known body to anatomize Among my household
summary: 'Anatomize' means to dissect for analysis — to cut open and examine part by part. Rumour is asking why it bothers to explain its own nature to those who already know it ('my household'). The word carries a faint sense of scholarly display; it is the same word used when someone says they will 'anatomize' a problem or lay it bare.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'anatomize' v. 2: 'To analyse or examine minutely; to lay bare as by dissection.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 21
OED s.v. 'anatomize' v. 2 ('to analyse or examine minutely') is a real sense that directly supports the gloss.
Reading 'anatomize' as to dissect or lay bare analytically is exact OED sense 2; the gloss accurately captures Rumour's rhetorical gesture without overreaching.

anchor_text: this worm-eaten hold of ragged stone, Where Hotspur's father, old Northumberland
summary: A 'hold' is an archaic word for a fortress or stronghold. The 'worm-eaten hold of ragged stone' is Warkworth Castle in Northumberland, the Percy family seat on the northeast coast of England. Northumberland has retreated there, claiming illness, instead of fighting alongside Hotspur at Shrewsbury. The crumbling description suits both the castle and the earl's failed courage.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): Northumberland's retreat from Shrewsbury to his northern strongholds.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'hold' n.: 'A fortified place, stronghold.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 35
Holinshed (1587) records Northumberland's retreat to his northern strongholds; Onions s.v. 'hold' as 'fortified place' is a standard gloss; both citations support the claims.
Identification of 'hold' as fortified stronghold and the location as Warkworth Castle (the Percy seat in Northumberland) is the consensus of all modern editors and is consistent with Holinshed.

anchor_text: Lies crafty-sick
summary: 'Crafty-sick' means sick by craft — faking illness as a deliberate strategy. Northumberland claimed he was too unwell to march to Shrewsbury and aid his son Hotspur; the rebels and historians (following Holinshed) suspected this was a convenient excuse to keep out of danger while waiting to see how the battle fell. The hyphenated compound makes the accusation impossible to miss.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): records Northumberland's plea of sickness as his reason for not joining the rebels at Shrewsbury.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 37

Holinshed (1587) records Northumberland's plea of sickness for his absence from Shrewsbury ('as some write, with all convenient speed'), directly supporting the claim that the chronicles record the sickness excuse.

'Crafty-sick' meaning sick by craft or feigning illness is the clear sense of the compound, and Northumberland's suspicious absence from Shrewsbury is grounded in Holinshed; the gloss does not overstate the ambiguity.

anchor_text: every minute now Should be the father of some stratagem
summary: A 'stratagem' in Elizabethan usage could mean a military maneuver or plan, but it also carried the stronger sense of a violent outrage or shocking deed — something treacherous or dreadful that happens in war. Northumberland means that in times this unstable, every minute may give birth to some new act of violence or political surprise.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'stratagem' 2: 'A violent or terrible deed; an act of cruelty or treachery' (citing numerous 16th–17th century instances).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 50

OED does list an obsolete sense of 'stratagem' as 'a violent or terrible deed' attested in 16th–17th century usage, but the exact sense number '2' could not be independently confirmed; the semantic claim is a real historical OED entry but the sense numbering may be imprecise.

The stronger Elizabethan sense of 'stratagem' as a violent outrage or shocking deed (OED sense 2) fits the context well; Northumberland's speech at TLN 50-54 is about the wildness of the times, making 'act of violence' the defensible primary reading here.

anchor_text: Harry Monmouth's brawn, the hulk Sir John, Is prisoner to your son
summary: 'Brawn' means a large, muscular lump of flesh (often applied to fattened swine fit for slaughter); 'hulk' was a big, unwieldy cargo-ship, used by extension for a massive, slow-moving body. Lord Bardolph's false report includes the claim that Falstaff has been captured by Hotspur. The insult-language — brawn, hulk — is the consistent way characters other than Hal and Falstaff himself refer to the fat knight.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'brawn' n. 1a: 'The flesh of a boar; flesh of any animal prepared for food.' OED s.v. 'hulk' n. 2b: 'A heavy, unwieldy person or thing.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 64
OED s.v. 'brawn' n. 1a and 'hulk' n. 2b are real senses that support the glosses; no factual overreach in the annotation.

'Brawn' as heavy animal flesh and 'hulk' as a large, unwieldy vessel or body are standard Elizabethan senses; the annotation correctly notes these are insult-terms applied to Falstaff by others, consistent with the play's pattern.

anchor_text: Since Caesar's fortunes!
summary: Lord Bardolph claims the (false) rebel victory at Shrewsbury is the greatest day since Julius Caesar's military campaigns — the benchmark for supreme conquest in the ancient world. The comparison is extravagant even in the lie: Caesar's campaigns in Gaul and the civil wars were the Roman world's standard for spectacular military success.
detail: The exclamation positions Shrewsbury as the equal of Caesar's greatest battles (Pharsalus, 48 BCE; the Gallic Wars, 58-50 BCE). The irony is that the comparison is founded entirely on Rumour's false report — a victory that did not happen. The allusion also reminds the audience that Shakespeare's Julius Caesar was likely on stage in the same period as Henry IV Part 2 (both c. 1598-99), making 'Caesar' a topical as well as classical reference.

sources.name: Plutarch, Lives (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Julius Caesar, in Sir Thomas North's translation (1579): Caesar's conquests as the measure of supreme military achievement.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 68

Plutarch's Life of Julius Caesar (North 1579) is a real text covering Caesar's conquests as the measure of supreme military achievement; the citation is accurate even if the annotation's claim is broadly framed.

The exclamation is defensible as a hyperbolic classical benchmark, but the detail suggesting a deliberate topical cross-reference to the stage-play Julius Caesar (c. 1599) is speculative — the phrase 'Caesar's fortunes' is a stock Elizabethan superlative, not necessarily a play-specific allusion, and the dating overlap is contested enough that this claim should be flagged.

anchor_text: young Harry Percy's spur was cold
summary: 'Spur was cold' is a euphemism for death by contrast: a spur, a sharp iron implement that drives a horse forward, suggests speed, heat, and life — 'Hotspur' was the nickname for Henry Percy because of his fiery, impetuous nature. To say his spur is 'cold' is to say the fire that drove him is out — he is dead. The pun runs through the next two lines when Northumberland bitterly echoes 'Of Hotspur Coldspur?'

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'cold': used of death and lifelessness (contrast 'hot' or 'warm').

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): Henry Percy nicknamed 'Hotspur' for his swift, impetuous valor.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 88
Onions s.v. 'cold' (death/lifelessness) and Holinshed's record of the 'Hotspur' nickname for Henry Percy are both real, confirmable references that support the wordplay gloss.
The hot/cold antithesis on 'spur' and 'Hotspur' is explicit in the text (Northumberland's next line directly inverts the name to 'Coldspur'), making the wordplay certain rather than merely inferred.

anchor_text: Of Hotspur Coldspur? that rebellion Had met ill luck?
summary: Northumberland turns the messenger's phrase into a bitter pun: 'Hotspur' was his son's famous nickname for his fiery impetuosity; 'Coldspur' is Northumberland's own invention, a name for a dead man whose fire is out. The coin-flip between the names is the moment the earl begins to suspect the truth. Shakespeare uses the same technique of pointed renaming to mark a death elsewhere — the living name becomes its opposite the moment life is extinguished.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'cold': 'wanting heat, especially as a sign of death.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 97
Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'cold' ('wanting heat, especially as a sign of death') is a real entry in a standard reference work and directly supports the gloss.

Northumberland's coinage 'Coldspur' as the death-antonym of 'Hotspur' is textually explicit and the interpretation that it marks the moment he begins to accept the truth is consistent with the dramatic action.

anchor_text: He was some hilding fellow that had stolen The horse he rode on
summary: 'Hilding' (also spelled 'hiding') is a word of contempt for a worthless, base, or cowardly person — someone beneath notice. Lord Bardolph dismisses the stranger on horseback who brought bad news as a low, valueless wretch who even stole the horse he was riding, and so cannot be trusted. It is bluster: he is trying to discredit news that contradicts his own false report.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'hilding' n. and adj.: 'A base, contemptible person; applied to persons of either sex; worthless.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 106
OED s.v. 'hilding' as 'a base, contemptible person; worthless' is a real entry that directly supports the gloss.
'Hilding' as a term of contempt for a worthless person is well-attested; the annotation correctly reads Lord Bardolph's motive as self-interested dismissal of contradicting news.

anchor_text: this man's brow, like to a title-leaf, Foretells the nature of a tragic volume
summary: Northumberland compares Morton's face to the title page of a book — in Elizabethan printing, a title page typically described the contents, so a grim face is compared to a page that announces the tragic story to follow. 'Volume' here means a book. The simile introduces a grieving messenger by saying his expression has already told the worst before he speaks a word.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'title-leaf' (rare): the title page of a book. Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'volume': 'a book.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 109
OED s.v. 'title-leaf' and Schmidt s.v. 'volume' are both real lexicographic references; the claim about Elizabethan title pages announcing contents is accurate.
The simile of a face as a title-page forecasting the contents of a tragic book is a natural extension of Elizabethan book-culture; the annotation's gloss is concise, accurate, and does not overreach.

anchor_text: Drew Priam's curtain in the dead of night, And would have told him half his Troy was burnt; But Priam found the fire ere he his tongue
summary: Priam was the aged king of Troy when the Greeks sacked and burned the city. Northumberland imagines a messenger stealing to Priam's bedside in the night to warn him that Troy was already half in flames — but finding that Priam already knew from the fire itself before any word was spoken. Northumberland draws the parallel to himself: he already reads Hotspur's death in Morton's face before Morton can say it.
detail: The fall of Troy was the great paradigm of disaster in the classical world; drawing a parallel to Priam and the burning city elevates Northumberland's personal grief to epic scale. 'Drew Priam's curtain' means pulled aside the bed-curtains — a four-poster bed in a great house had heavy curtains drawn around it at night. The vividness of the image (the messenger parting the curtain, the glow of fire already visible) is Shakespeare's own invention, not a specific source passage, but it draws on the Troy tradition available through Virgil, Ovid, and North's Plutarch.

sources.name: Virgil, Aeneid
sources.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 2.506-558 (the sack of Troy and Priam's death at the altar): the primary ancient source for the Troy narrative and Priam's end.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 122

Virgil Aeneid 2.506-558 is confirmed to cover Priam's death during the sack of Troy at those exact lines; the annotation correctly notes the specific imagery is Shakespeare's own invention built on the classical tradition.

The Priam/Troy parallel is clearly signaled by Shakespeare himself in the text; attributing the specific curtain image to Virgil Aeneid 2 is reasonable (though Virgil does not show the messenger drawing the bedcurtain — this detail is Shakespeare's own invention, as the annotation itself acknowledges), so the gloss correctly stops short of claiming a specific source passage.

anchor_text: the first bringer of unwelcome news Hath but a losing office, and his tongue Sounds ever after as a sullen bell, Remember'd tolling a departing friend
summary: Northumberland develops a simile: a messenger who first brings bad news carries a 'losing office' (a role that costs him, not gains him). His voice becomes like a 'sullen bell' — 'sullen' here means mournful and slow-tolling, not sulky. A 'departing friend' is a friend who is dying; church bells were rung slowly to mark a death (called a 'passing bell' or 'knell'). The image means the messenger's voice is forever after associated in the listener's memory only with grief.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'sullen' adj. 3: 'Of sounds: slow and heavy, mournful.' OED s.v. 'departing' vbl. n.: 'dying, death' (archaic).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 151
OED s.v. 'sullen' adj. 3 ('slow and heavy, mournful') and 'departing' vbl. n. ('dying, death') are real senses that directly support the gloss.

'Sullen' as slow and mournful (of a bell), 'departing friend' as a dying person, and 'losing office' as a role that costs the holder are all established Elizabethan senses that fit the text precisely.

anchor_text: Rendering faint quittance, wearied and outbreathed
summary: 'Quittance' means return, repayment, or requital — here specifically the return of blows in combat, i.e. fighting back. 'Rendering faint quittance' means giving back only weak and feeble resistance. 'Outbreathed' means out of breath, exhausted. Morton is describing Hotspur in his final moments: barely able to strike back at Prince Hal, out of wind and strength.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'quittance' n. 2: 'Requital; return, repayment (of blows, injuries, etc.).' OED s.v. 'outbreathed' ppl. adj.: 'Out of breath; exhausted.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 159
OED s.v. 'quittance' n. 2 ('requital; return of blows') and 'outbreathed' ppl. adj. ('out of breath') are real entries that directly support the gloss.

'Quittance' as requital of blows in combat and 'outbreathed' as exhausted are exact OED senses; the reading that Morton describes Hotspur barely fighting back before death is confirmed by the text at TLN 159-162.

anchor_text: whose well-labouring sword Had three times slain the appearance of the king
summary: At Shrewsbury, Henry IV had several noblemen dressed in full royal armor to confuse and protect him — decoys wearing 'the appearance of the king.' The Douglas killed three of them one by one, thinking each time he had slain the real king, before finally encountering the actual Henry. This tactic of royal doubles was historical practice in medieval battle.
detail: Holinshed records that 'the king that daie did fight with great regard of his safetie,' and that several knights dressed in the king's coat were slain. Shakespeare dramatizes this in Henry IV Part 1, where the Douglas kills Blunt in the king's coat. Morton's report here confirms the historical detail. The phrase 'the appearance of the king' — the semblance, the visible likeness — carries thematic weight in plays so concerned with the difference between surface and reality.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): the Battle of Shrewsbury, knights dressed in the king's coat as decoys, and Douglas killing several of them.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 178

Holinshed (1587) records knights dressed in the king's coat as decoys at Shrewsbury and Douglas slaying several of them, confirmed by multiple sources including the Internet Shakespeare Editions Holinshed selection.

The royal-decoy tactic at Shrewsbury is recorded in Holinshed and dramatized in 1 Henry IV (Blunt killed in the king's coat); Morton's account here is consistent with that dramatization, and the annotation does not overstate.

anchor_text: 'Gan vail his stomach and did grace the shame Of those that turn'd their backs
summary: 'Gan' is an archaic form of 'began.' 'Vail' means to lower or let fall (from Old French aval, downward) — so 'vail his stomach' means to lower his pride or courage ('stomach' in Elizabethan English often meant courage or pride). To 'grace the shame' of the fleeing men means to dignify — or rather make slightly less disgraceful — the rout, by the great Douglas fleeing alongside them. Even the fearless Douglas ran.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'vail' v.1 1: 'To lower; to let fall (the eyes, head, a flag, etc.).' OED s.v. 'stomach' n. 6: 'Spirit, courage, pride.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 180
OED s.v. 'vail' v.1 1 ('to lower; to let fall') and 'stomach' n. 6 ('spirit, courage, pride') are real senses that directly support the glosses; etymology from Old French 'aval' is correct.

'Gan' as archaic preterite of 'begin,' 'vail' as to lower, and 'stomach' as courage or pride are all exact Elizabethan senses; the reading that even Douglas fled (gracing the shame of others) is confirmed by TLN 180-182.

anchor_text: thou nice crutch! A scaly gauntlet now with joints of steel Must glove this hand: and hence, thou sickly quoif!
summary: Northumberland casts away the props of illness and old age. 'Nice' here means delicate or soft, not pleasant; a 'quoif' (also spelled coif) is a close-fitting linen cap worn by the sick, the elderly, and lawyers indoors — a sign of infirmity and retreat from active life. A 'gauntlet' is an armored glove of overlapping metal scales ('scaly'). The theatrical gesture of throwing off the sick-man's cap and calling for a gauntlet announces that Northumberland intends to fight.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'quoif' (coif) n. 1: 'A close-fitting cap covering the top, back, and sides of the head.' OED s.v. 'nice' adj. 3: 'Delicate, fragile, frail.' OED s.v. 'gauntlet' n. 1: 'An armored glove.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 196
OED s.v. 'quoif'/'coif' n. 1, 'nice' adj. 3, and 'gauntlet' n. 1 are all real OED entries with the senses cited; the description of a coif as worn by the sick and elderly is accurate.

'Nice' as delicate/frail, 'quoif/coif' as a close-fitting invalid's or lawyer's cap, and 'gauntlet' as an armored glove are all correct; the reading of the gesture as theatrical casting-off of the sick-man's props is exactly right and is what the stage direction implies.

anchor_text: one spirit of the first-born Cain Reign in all bosoms
summary: In Genesis, Cain was the first-born son of Adam and Eve, and the first murderer — he killed his brother Abel out of envy. Northumberland, consumed with rage and grief over Hotspur's death, invokes Cain's spirit of murderous violence, wishing it would possess all humanity. It is a call for universal war and slaughter: let the instinct of the first killer rule every heart.
detail: The invocation of Cain as the spirit of all human violence is the extreme pitch of Northumberland's grief-speech. Coming immediately after his order for nature to dissolve ('Let heaven kiss earth!... let order die!'), the Cain allusion caps a vision of total chaos — the great chain of being unmade, God's ordained order destroyed, and fratricide's spirit enthroned. Northumberland in effect wishes for the very apocalypse. His allies Travers and Lord Bardolph immediately pull him back from the edge.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Genesis 4:1-16 (Geneva 1599): Cain kills Abel; God sets a curse on him.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 208
Genesis 4:1-16 in the Geneva Bible (1599) covers Cain killing Abel and the curse; this is a real, verifiable passage that supports the allusion as described.

The allusion to Cain as the first murderer and the reading of Northumberland's speech as a wish for universal violence are correct; situating it as the apex of the chaos-wish ('let order die') within the de casibus pattern is a defensible and mainstream interpretive frame.

anchor_text: the gentle Archbishop of York is up With well-appointed powers: he is a man Who with a double surety binds his followers
summary: 'Is up' means has risen in rebellion, is in arms. Richard Scroop, Archbishop of York, is the new leader of the northern uprising after Shrewsbury. 'Well-appointed' means fully equipped and organized. A 'double surety' means a twofold bond of loyalty: the Archbishop holds his followers with both the authority of the Church and the promise of a political grievance — two ropes to bind one man, far stronger than Hotspur's purely military cause.
detail: Morton's strategic point is that the Archbishop can recruit where Hotspur could not: soldiers who feared that rebellion against the king was a sin found their consciences quieted when a senior churchman told them the cause was holy. 'Gentle' here means noble-born, not mild-tempered. Scroop was the Archbishop of York from 1398 until his execution in 1405 following the collapse of the Gaultree rebellion in this play. Shakespeare follows Holinshed closely on his role.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): Richard Scroop, Archbishop of York, joins the Percy rebellion after Shrewsbury and leads the northern lords.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 240

Holinshed (1587) records Archbishop Scroop joining the Percy rebellion after Shrewsbury; Scroop was Archbishop of York from 1398 until his execution in 1405 after the Gaultree/Shipton Moor episode, as confirmed by multiple historical sources.

Identifying Richard Scroop as Archbishop of York, reading 'is up' as in armed rebellion, and explaining 'double surety' as the twofold bond of church authority plus political grievance are all well-grounded in Holinshed and in the text itself (TLN 251-254 spells out the religious dimension explicitly).

anchor_text: doth enlarge his rising with the blood Of fair King Richard, scraped from Pomfret stones
summary: The Archbishop strengthens his rebellion by invoking the murder of Richard II, the king Henry IV deposed and who died (almost certainly murdered) at Pontefract Castle in Yorkshire — 'Pomfret' is the old English pronunciation of Pontefract. 'Scraped from Pomfret stones' is a grim image: the spilled blood of the murdered king still staining the castle stones, as though it could never be washed away. The Archbishop uses Richard's blood as a rallying cry against Bolingbroke.
detail: Pontefract (Pomfret) Castle in West Yorkshire was where Richard II was held after his deposition and where he died in early 1400 — the chronicles leave his exact fate uncertain, but murder or deliberate starvation were widely assumed. The Archbishop of York's use of Richard's blood as a legitimizing grievance is historically significant: it gives the rebellion a moral and quasi-sacred dimension beyond mere factional ambition, painting Henry IV as a usurper with blood on his hands. Shakespeare dramatized Richard's death at Pomfret in Richard II (5.5).

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): Richard II kept and dying at Pontefract Castle, c. February 1400.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 255

Holinshed (1587) records Richard II's death at Pontefract (Pomfret) Castle around February 1400; the castle's location in West Yorkshire and the historical circumstances of Richard's captivity and death are accurately described.

'Pomfret' as the English form of Pontefract is correct; the reading that the Archbishop uses Richard's death as a moral legitimizing grievance is directly stated in the text ('enlarge his rising with the blood / Of fair King Richard'), and the annotation accurately reflects Holinshed's uncertainty about the manner of Richard's death.

anchor_text: what says the doctor to my water
summary: Uroscopy — diagnosing illness by examining a patient's urine — was the standard first step in Elizabethan medicine. Falstaff has sent a sample ('his water') to a physician for inspection; the doctor can read color, sediment, and smell for signs of disease. The Page's reply that the patient 'might have moe diseases than he knew for' is an understated verdict on Falstaff's debauchery.

anchor_text: I have read the cause of his effects in Galen
summary: Galen (Claudius Galenus, c. 129-216 CE) was the Greek physician whose theories dominated European medicine for over 1,400 years. OED s.v. 'puissance' is a real entry confirming the Old French derivation and the senses of military/political power cited in the summary.
The hendiadys reading of 'power and puissance' as a rhetorical intensifier is sound and mainstream; the pronunciation gloss and Old French derivation are accurate.

anchor_text: young Hotspur's case at Shrewsbury
summary: Hotspur (Henry Percy) led the first Percy rebellion against Henry IV and was defeated and killed at the Battle of Shrewsbury on 21 July 1403. His fatal mistake — fighting before his ally Northumberland arrived with reinforcements — is exactly the cautionary tale Lord Bardolph raises here. This play begins in the immediate aftermath of Shrewsbury, where the rebels are now regrouping under the Archbishop of York.
detail: The events of Henry IV Part 1 are the backstory of this scene: Hotspur advanced to battle expecting Northumberland's troops and Glendower's Welsh army to join him, but both were absent when the fighting started. Henry IV crushed the rebel force; Hotspur died (the play attributes his death to Prince Hal in single combat). Northumberland's failure to march his forces to Shrewsbury — whether from illness or calculation — haunts the new revolt. The Archbishop and his lords now face the same question: can they act without Northumberland?

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the Battle of Shrewsbury, 21 July 1403.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 490
Holinshed Chronicles (1587) does record the Battle of Shrewsbury (21 July 1403), Northumberland's absence due to illness, and Hotspur's death in the engagement — all consistent with the claims made.

The historical gloss is accurate and directly supported by the text: the Archbishop himself names Hotspur's case as the cautionary parallel, and the account of absent allies matches Part 1's dramatised events.

anchor_text: lined himself with hope, Eating the air on promise of supply
summary: 'Lined himself with hope' means he armored or stuffed himself with false confidence — 'lined' as in a coat lined with padding, but hollow. 'Eating the air' is a proverbial image for feeding on nothing, living on illusion: Hotspur gorged on the promise of troops that never came, the way a starving man might try to eat wind. The phrase comes from a French proverbial expression ('paitre de vent') meaning to sustain oneself on empty promises.
detail: Lord Bardolph's speech compresses Hotspur's disaster into a compact sequence of images: lining (false armor), eating air (hollow nourishment), flattering himself, and a power 'much smaller than the smallest of his thoughts.' The climax — 'winking leap'd into destruction' (TLN 497) — means he shut his eyes and jumped blindly. 'Winking' in Elizabethan English means closing the eyes, not a facial tic; the image is of a man who willfully stops looking at reality.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A. Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'line' (v., sense 3: to reinforce, to fill out) and s.v. 'winking' (adj.: with eyes shut, blindly).

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'eat the air': to subsist on vain hopes.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 491

Schmidt and Onions are real references and support the word-sense claims, but the summary asserts the phrase derives from a French proverbial expression ('paitre de vent') with no cited source for that claim, making it an unsourced gloss embedded among real citations.

'Lined himself with hope' as false armour/padding is the standard reading, 'eating the air' as hollow sustenance is well-attested, and 'winking' as eyes-shut is correct Elizabethan usage; no over-reading detected.

anchor_text: When we mean to build, We first survey the plot, then draw the model
summary: Lord Bardolph extends a single comparison — planning a rebellion is like planning a building — for twenty-two lines, one of the longest sustained metaphors in the play. 'Survey the plot' means measure the land; 'draw the model' means draft the architectural plan; 'rate the cost of the erection' means calculate expenses; 'offices' are rooms. If the money does not match the ambition, you build a smaller house — or nothing at all. The rebels, Bardolph argues, must do the same realistic accounting of their forces.
detail: This figure is an 'extended metaphor' or 'allegory by conceit': a single vehicle (house-building) is mapped systematically onto a tenor (military planning) through multiple matching terms. The argument concludes at TLN 520-521: 'We fortify in paper and in figures, / Using the names of men instead of men' — meaning on paper they have an army; in reality they may have only numbers. A 'naked subject to the weeping clouds' (TLN 525) is a half-built skeleton of a house, exposed to rain — an image for a rebellion launched without sufficient forces and left vulnerable to a stronger enemy.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'model', n., sense 5a: a ground plan or design of a building; s.v. 'office', n., sense 20: a room in a house serving a particular domestic function.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 505
OED senses for 'model' (n., architectural ground plan) and 'office' (n., domestic room) are real and accurately characterised.

The identification of this as an extended metaphor mapping house-building onto military planning is accurate and textually grounded; 'offices' as domestic rooms and 'model' as ground-plan are correct Elizabethan senses.

anchor_text: his divisions, as the times do brawl, Are in three heads: one power against the French, And one against Glendower
summary: Hastings maps the strategic situation that gives the rebels their opening: Henry IV is fighting three separate wars at once. One English army holds the French border (the French under Charles VI were a perennial threat and had recently supported the Welsh revolt). A second fights Owain Glendower, the Welsh chieftain who had been in open rebellion since 1400. The third must now face the Archbishop's northern rising — so no single front can receive overwhelming force.
detail: Owain Glendower (Owen Glendower in Shakespeare, 'Glendwr' in Welsh) had led a major Welsh revolt from 1400 onward, allying at one point with Hotspur and the Mortimer family — as dramatized in Henry IV Part 1. By the time of the Archbishop's rebellion, Glendower's revolt was weakening but not finished. The French threat was partly diplomatic, partly tied to Welsh alliances: Charles VI had sent troops to Wales in 1405. Hastings's point is arithmetical: a kingdom fighting on three fronts simultaneously cannot concentrate its resources against any one enemy.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Owain Glendower's revolt (1400-c.1410) and Anglo-French hostilities in the early years of Henry IV's reign.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 534

Holinshed (1587) covers both the Glendower revolt from 1400 and Anglo-French hostilities; the French expedition to Wales in 1405 under Charles VI is independently confirmed and within the period Holinshed addresses.

Hastings's claim that Henry faces simultaneous French, Welsh, and northern threats is presented as fact, but historically the French front at this precise moment (c. 1405) is more equivocal than the gloss allows — the French sent forces to Wales rather than engaging England directly; calling it a separate 'front' risks overstating what is really a Welsh-French allied pressure, though the dramatic logic of the scene supports the three-way split as Hastings sees it.

anchor_text: The commonwealth is sick of their own choice; Their over-greedy love hath surfeited
summary: 'Surfeited' means made sick by excess — the same word used when someone overeats to the point of nausea. 'The vulgar heart' (TLN 556) means the heart of the common people: 'vulgar' here carries no insult beyond 'common' or 'ordinary' — from Latin vulgus (the crowd). The Archbishop's argument is that the people cheered Bolingbroke (now Henry IV) so extravagantly that they have made themselves ill on him, the way a person gorges on something and then cannot stand it.
detail: The disease metaphor ('commonwealth is sick') and the gluttony metaphor ('surfeited') are being fused here and will run through the next eight lines. 'Commonwealth' is the political body of the realm — all its subjects considered as a collective. The Archbishop positions the rebellion as a kind of cure or purge, since the body politic has eaten too much of the current king.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'surfeit', v., sense 1: to be satiated to the point of disgust or sickness.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A. Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'vulgar' (adj., sense 1: of or belonging to the common people; not pejorative in itself).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 553
OED s.v. 'surfeit' and Schmidt s.v. 'vulgar' are real, standard references whose cited senses accurately support the summary claims.

'Vulgar' as common/ordinary without pejorative force and 'surfeited' as sick from excess are both standard Elizabethan senses, correctly glossed; the disease-plus-gluttony fusion is plainly in the text.

anchor_text: O thou fond many, with what loud applause Didst thou beat heaven with blessing Bolingbroke
summary: 'Fond many' means the foolish multitude — 'fond' in Elizabethan English means foolish or infatuated, not affectionate. 'Beat heaven with blessing' means that the crowd's cheering was so loud it hammered the sky with noise. The Archbishop then calls the populace a 'beastly feeder' and a 'common dog,' building an extended image of the crowd as an animal that gorged itself on the idea of Bolingbroke, then 'cast him up' (vomited) and now howls to get back what it spat out.
detail: This passage is one of the play's sharpest pieces of political commentary. The Archbishop — a churchman leading a rebellion — is essentially arguing that popular consent is worthless precisely because it is fickle: the crowd that screamed for Bolingbroke to depose Richard now mourns Richard. 'Cast him up' (TLN 562) is an unflinching metaphor for vomiting: the crowd stuffed itself with Bolingbroke, became sick, regurgitated him as king, and now tries to lap up the vomit — only to find it gone. The contempt for mob sentiment here mirrors a widespread Elizabethan fear of popular political instability.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A. Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'fond' (adj., sense 1: foolish, infatuated; not 'affectionate'); s.v. 'cast up' (to vomit).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 557
Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon does record 'fond' as foolish/infatuated and 'cast up' as to vomit — both senses are well-attested in standard Shakespeare lexicography.

'Fond' as foolish rather than affectionate is the correct Elizabethan sense, 'beat heaven with blessing' as thunderous noise is sound, and 'cast him up' as vomit is the unambiguous meaning; the political commentary on mob fickleness is the plain drift of the Archbishop's speech.

anchor_text: thou common dog, didst thou disgorge Thy glutton bosom of the royal Richard
summary: The Archbishop recalls the London crowd's behaviour at the moment of Richard II's public humiliation in 1399: they pelted him with dirt ('threw'st dust upon his goodly head') as Bolingbroke led him through the streets a prisoner. The Archbishop — speaking as if directly to the crowd — reminds them that they cheered Richard's fall, and now they grieve for him. This eyewitness detail comes directly from historical sources and was shown on stage in Richard II.
detail: Holinshed records that on the day Richard was brought into London behind Bolingbroke, the crowd threw garbage at the captive king. Shakespeare staged this moment in Richard II (5.2), where York describes the scene — Richard riding through proud London, the crowd hurling 'dust and rubbish' on his 'sacred head' while roaring for Bolingbroke. The Archbishop's speech here is a callback to that humiliation, and his point is precise: the very same people who degraded Richard in the street are now weeping for him. The phrase 'glutton bosom' continues the feeding/disgorgement metaphor: the crowd's chest (its appetite, its inner self) was crammed full of Richard and had to vomit him out.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Henry Bolingbroke's entry into London with the captive Richard II, 1399.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 563

Holinshed (1587) records Bolingbroke's triumphal London entry with the captive Richard, and the crowd throwing refuse on Richard is corroborated by Richard II 5.2 ('Threw dust and rubbish on King Richard's head'), which is itself drawn from Holinshed — the citation is appropriate.

The recall of the London crowd throwing dust on Richard is directly stated in the text ('threw'st dust upon his goodly head') and corroborated by Holinshed and by Richard II 5.2; calling it an 'eyewitness detail' overstates certainty (it is a literary-historical tradition) but does not distort the gloss.

anchor_text: Past and to come seems best; things present worst
summary: This single line is an aphorism — a tightly compressed general truth — delivered as the Archbishop's conclusion. Its form is a chiasmus: past and future flank 'best,' while 'present' stands alone as 'worst.' The observation is that people habitually idealize what they no longer have (Richard) and what they have not yet received (some better future), while resenting whatever they actually possess right now (Henry IV). It is a bitter summary of human political psychology: the crowd can never be content with the present.
detail: The chiastic structure (A-B / B-A inversion) is characteristic of Shakespeare's sententious or aphoristic lines and helps make the statement feel weighty and permanent. As the Archbishop ends his denunciation, the line functions as a couplet-like clincher, lifting from the specific case of Richard and Bolingbroke to a universal principle. It also has an ironic application to the rebels themselves: they are trusting in the hope of a better future ('past and to come seems best') rather than reckoning with present difficulty.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'seems' (used impersonally: 'it seems'). The aphoristic compression is noted by Humphreys, A. R. (ed.), The Second Part of King Henry IV, Arden 2 (1966), note to 4.1.101 [TLN 574].

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 574

The Onions citation for 'seems' is real but does not address the chiasmus or aphorism noted in the summary; the Humphreys Arden 2 note is cited as '4.1.101 [TLN 574]' — this line sits in 1.3 by most modern lineations and the act/scene reference cannot be independently verified, raising doubt about the note locus.

The aphorism is correctly identified and the chiasmus reading is accurate (past/future framed as best, present as worst); the ironic application to the rebels themselves is a defensible and non-forced observation.

anchor_text: We are time's subjects, and time bids be gone
summary: Hastings ends the scene with a compact personification: Time is their lord, and they are its subjects — the same political word ('subjects') used for a king's obedient vassals. Because they serve Time, they must obey its command to leave now. The line draws an implicit contrast with the rebels' other lord, the king against whom they are marching: they may be rebels against Henry IV, but they are still subject to Time.
detail: The paradox in the final line is gentle but pointed. The rebels are asserting their autonomy against one king while submitting to another master — Time — who cannot be defied. 'Subject' in Elizabethan English was the normal word for a person under the authority of a monarch, so calling themselves 'time's subjects' carries a political charge that a modern audience might miss. As a closing epigram it recalls the play's larger meditation on time: an aging king, a rebellion rooted in old grievances, and a prince who has not yet become himself.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A. Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'subject' (n., sense 1: one who owes allegiance and obedience to a sovereign). Personification of Time as ruler is a commonplace of Elizabethan poetry: cf. Sonnet 60 ('Like as the waves make towards the pebbled shore, / So do our minutes hasten to their end').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 576

Schmidt s.v. 'subject' is a real entry; the cross-reference to Sonnet 60 ('Like as the waves make towards the pebbled shore') is accurate — it is the opening of Sonnet 60 and concerns time's dominion.

'Subject' carrying its political valence of allegiance to a sovereign is correct Elizabethan usage, and the gentle paradox of rebels submitting to Time while defying the king is a defensible and restrained reading that does not overreach.

anchor_text: have you entered the action
summary: To 'enter the action' is a legal phrase meaning to file the formal record of a lawsuit in court. Mistress Quickly has gone to a law officer — Fang — to initiate legal proceedings against Falstaff for his unpaid debts.
detail: An 'action' in Elizabethan common law was the formal claim brought before a court; to 'enter' it was to register it in the official record so that it could proceed. The word 'entered' is repeated at TLN 578 (Fang) and TLN 584 (the Hostess), who uses it again for Falstaff himself — 'I have entered him and all' — garbling the sense so that she has 'entered' both the action and the defendant as though they were the same thing. Her confusion of legal vocabulary is characteristic of her throughout the scene.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'action,' n. 14a: 'A legal process or suit; a proceeding by one party against another before a court of law.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 577

OED does carry a legal sense for 'action' (a suit or proceeding before a court) and the sub-sense cited ('n. 14a') is consistent with the OED's numbering system for this entry; the substance is accurate and uncontroversial.

The legal sense of 'enter the action' is well-supported by the scene's explicit debt-collection context, and the annotation correctly identifies Quickly's comic confusion of 'entering' both the action and the defendant as a malapropistic garbling of legal vocabulary.

anchor_text: lusty yeoman? will 'a stand to 't
summary: Mistress Quickly asks whether Fang's assistant is a 'lusty' (vigorous, robust) yeoman — a minor law officer — and whether he will 'stand to it,' meaning hold his ground against Falstaff. Both phrases carry sexual double meanings that she is almost certainly not aware of: 'lusty' also means sexually vigorous, and 'stand to it' is common Elizabethan slang for sexual readiness.
detail: A 'yeoman' in this context is a sergeant's assistant or bailiff; the word had no bawdy meaning. 'Lusty,' however, was routinely used in sexual senses (OED s.v. 'lusty,' 2), and 'stand to it' appears in bawdy contexts throughout the period. The comedy turns on Mistress Quickly's obliviousness: she means only 'will he be brave enough,' but her phrasing gives the scene its characteristic undercurrent. The same pattern runs through her speech at TLN 585-592, where 'thrust,' 'foin,' 'close,' and 'elbow' accumulate sexual overtones that the speakers do not notice but the audience does.

sources.name: Williams, Glossary of Shakespeare's Sexual Language
sources.citation: Gordon Williams, A Glossary of Shakespeare's Sexual Language (1997), s.v. 'lusty,' 'stand.'

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'lusty,' adj. 2: 'Full of lust or desire; lascivious, wanton.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 579

Gordon Williams's work on Shakespeare's sexual language is real (published as 'Shakespeare's Sexual Language: A Glossary,' Athlone/Continuum, with editions from the 1990s); OED 'lusty' adj. 2 for the lascivious sense is attested; both sources support the bawdy reading.

Both the primary meaning (vigorous sergeant's assistant) and the bawdy undercurrent ('lusty' as sexually vigorous, 'stand to it' as sexual readiness) are well-attested in Elizabethan usage, and the annotation correctly emphasises Quickly's obliviousness rather than claiming intentional wordplay on her part.

anchor_text: he will foin like any devil
summary: To 'foin' means to thrust with a pointed weapon, particularly a sword or dagger. Mistress Quickly warns that Falstaff stabs without mercy — 'he will foin like any devil' — and will not spare man, woman, or child.
detail: The verb 'foin' (also spelled 'foyne' or 'foine') derives from the Old French 'foigner,' to thrust; it was standard fencing vocabulary in Shakespeare's England for a straight lunge with the point of a blade, as opposed to a slashing cut. The word's disappearance from English by the eighteenth century makes this line opaque to modern readers. Snare's fear that the arrest 'may chance cost some of our lives, for he will stab' (TLN 585) is confirmed by Quickly's graphic account: the fat knight had already stabbed her in her own house.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'foin,' v.: 'To thrust with a sword or lance; to lunge.' First attested in the 14th century, largely obsolete after the 17th.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'foin': 'to thrust, to push forward with a lance.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 588

OED 'foin' v. is a real entry attested from c.1380 meaning to thrust with a pointed weapon; Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real reference work and does include 'foin'; both sources support the gloss.

'Foin' as a fencing term for a thrust is unambiguous and well-documented in period sources; the scene's context of Falstaff's threatened violence confirms the reading, and the annotation makes no over-claim.

anchor_text: an 'a come but within my vice
summary: A 'vice' here is a mechanical gripping device — a screw-clamp or hand-vice — used by craftsmen to hold an object fast. Fang means: if Falstaff comes close enough to grab, he will hold him in a grip as tight as that of a bench-vice.
detail: The word 'vice' (also spelled 'vise') for a clamping tool is unrelated to moral vice; both derive ultimately from Latin 'vitis' (vine-shoot, then spiral or screw). Fang is a sergeant — a low law officer — and his boast is physical: his grip, once closed, will not release. The image also implies the mechanics of arrest: a sergeant could lawfully seize a debtor, and the debtor who physically escaped could sometimes avoid legal process.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'vice,' n.3, 1: 'An instrument of iron or wood, having two jaws which are closed by means of a screw... used by smiths and other craftsmen for gripping objects.'

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'vice' (tool): the clamping sense distinguished from the moral one.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 592
OED 'vice' n.3 for the clamping tool is a well-documented entry; Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is real and distinguishes the tool sense from the moral sense; both sources correctly support the gloss.
The tool-vice sense is the only viable reading here — the text is Fang's boast about his grip — and the derivation and legal context around a sergeant's right to seize a debtor are correctly stated.

anchor_text: infinitive thing upon my score
summary: 'Infinitive' is Mistress Quickly's mangled form of 'infinite' — she means Falstaff owes her an enormous, uncountable debt. A 'score' is a tally of credit: tavern-keepers kept account of what drinkers owed by cutting notches in a stick of wood. She is saying his debt on her tally is beyond counting.
detail: Quickly's speech is riddled with malapropisms — wrong words that sound vaguely like the right ones. 'Infinitive' is the grammatical term for a verb form; 'infinite' is what she needs (OED s.v. 'infinite': boundless, unlimited). The error is comic but also characterizes her voice throughout the play. 'Score' as a tallying device is the source of the modern sense of keeping score: the word comes from Old Norse 'skor,' a notch or incision. Tavern credit was a standard institution — drinkers ran up scores, and landlords pursued them in court exactly as the Hostess does here.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'score,' n. 4a: 'A notch or incision cut in wood as a record; a reckoning or account kept by cutting notches.' Sense 4b extends to any record of credit or debt.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911, rev. Eagleson 1986), s.v. 'score': 'account.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 594

OED 'score' n.4a for a notch cut in wood as a tally is confirmed (Old Norse 'skor'); Onions's Shakespeare Glossary is a real work (1911, rev. Eagleson 1986) and does gloss 'score' as 'account'; both sources support the claim.
'Infinitive' for 'infinite' is a standard Quickly malapropism, and 'score' as a tally-stick debt record is exactly right for the tavern context; both readings are uncontroversial.

anchor_text: continuantly to Pie-corner--saving your manhoods--to buy a saddle; and he is indited to dinner to the Lubber's-head in Lumbert Street
summary: Pie-corner was a real London street corner at Giltspur Street and Cock Lane in Smithfield, famous for cook-shops and meat-pies, near butchers' stalls. 'Lombard Street' (garbled by Quickly as 'Lumbert Street') was the main street of London's Italian banking and merchant community. Both locations fix the scene firmly in the working-class geography of the city.
detail: Pie-corner was associated with cheap food and prostitution; Quickly's awkward aside 'saving your manhoods' may acknowledge that the neighborhood had a dubious reputation. 'Indited' is Quickly's malapropism for 'invited' — one of several she produces in this speech. The Lubber's-head in Lombard Street is unidentified, likely a fictional tavern named for a leopard's head (a heraldic device), which Quickly could easily confuse with 'lubber' (a clumsy oaf). Lombard Street took its name from the Italian Lombard bankers who settled there from the thirteenth century; it remained the financial centre of the city in Shakespeare's day.

sources.name: Stow, Survey of London (1598)
sources.citation: John Stow, A Survey of London (1598), on Pie-corner (Giltspur Street corner) and Lombard Street.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'indite': Quickly's malapropism for 'invite.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 595

Stow's Survey of London (1598) is confirmed to describe Pie-corner at the north end of Giltspur Street in Smithfield and to record Lombard Street's Italian Lombard banking history; both topographical claims are supported by Stow.

Both London locations are accurately identified, 'indited' for 'invited' is a standard Quickly malapropism, and the annotation appropriately hedges on the Lubber's-head as an unidentified (likely fictional) tavern rather than asserting it as historical fact; the leopard's-head heraldic gloss for 'lubber' is speculative but flagged as such.

anchor_text: A hundred mark is a long one for a poor lone woman to bear
summary: A 'mark' was a unit of account worth two-thirds of a pound (13 shillings and 4 pence). One hundred marks equalled just over sixty-six pounds — a very large sum for a tavern-keeper: roughly a skilled tradesman's income for several years. Mistress Quickly's claim makes clear how seriously Falstaff has exploited her.
detail: The mark was not a coin but a money of account used in England since the medieval period, fixed at 160 silver pence (two-thirds of a pound sterling of 240 pence). In Shakespeare's England, a master craftsman might earn perhaps ten to twenty pounds a year; sixty-six pounds was therefore a ruinous debt for a widowed innkeeper. The sum recurs in Part 1 and Part 2 as the scale of Falstaff's predation on the Hostess. Shakespeare is careful with such numbers: a hundred marks is enough to make the lawsuit plausible and the Hostess's distress real.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'mark,' n.2, 4: 'A money of account in England, equal to 13s. 4d., or two-thirds of a pound sterling.'

sources.name: Keeton, Shakespeare's Legal and Political Background
sources.citation: George W. Keeton, Shakespeare's Legal and Political Background (1967), ch. 10, on debt actions in the Elizabethan courts.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 600

OED 'mark' n.2 for 13s 4d is confirmed; Keeton's 'Shakespeare's Legal and Political Background' (1967) is a real book covering debt law, but 'ch. 10 on debt actions in the Elizabethan courts' is a specific chapter attribution that cannot be externally verified and may be invented.
The mark as two-thirds of a pound (13s 4d) is correct, and the relative magnitude — ruinous for a widowed tavern-keeper — is appropriately contextualized without over-reading the dramatic stakes.

anchor_text: arrant malmsey-nose knave, Bardolph
summary: Malmsey was a rich, dark-red sweet wine imported from Greece and Madeira. Calling Bardolph a 'malmsey-nose' knave is an insult for his famously red, inflamed nose, which the play associates throughout with his heavy drinking. Bardolph's fiery face is a running joke in both parts of Henry IV.
detail: Malvasia (malmsey) wine ranged in color from deep amber to dark red; the term for Bardolph's nose collapses his drinking habit into his physical appearance. Bardolph's nose and face are compared to a burning lamp (Part 1 3.3), to hellfire, and to the rich man Dives burning in hell (Part 1 3.3 — see the Dives and Lazarus reference card). The joke that his complexion saves candle-money appears as early as Part 1 1.2. Here Mistress Quickly uses it as a term of abuse — 'arrant' means thoroughgoing or out-and-out (OED s.v. 'arrant': 'downright, thoroughgoing, unmitigated').

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'malmsey,' n.: 'A strong sweet wine, originally from Greece, later also from Madeira and the Canaries.' s.v. 'arrant,' adj.: 'Downright, thoroughgoing (used to intensify a term of reproach).'

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'malmsey': 'a sort of rich, sweet wine.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 606

OED 'malmsey' n. for the sweet Greek/Madeiran wine is real; OED 'arrant' adj. for 'downright, thoroughgoing' is real; Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon does include 'malmsey'; all sources support the gloss.
Malmsey as a dark sweet wine giving its name to Bardolph's red nose is the standard reading, consistent with the running nose-and-drink jokes throughout both Henry IV parts; no over-reach is present.

anchor_text: thou honey-suckle villain! wilt thou kill God's officers and the king's? Ah, thou honey-seed rogue! thou art a honey-seed, a man-queller, and a woman-queller
summary: Mistress Quickly is reaching for the word 'homicidal' — meaning a killer — and garbles it into 'honey-suckle' and 'honey-seed,' which are the names of harmless plants. 'Man-queller' and 'woman-queller' are her own coinages meaning 'man-killer' and 'woman-killer': to 'quell' means to kill or destroy.
detail: The malapropism is a sustained comic set-piece. Quickly wants to call Falstaff a 'homicide' (killer) and a 'homicidal' rogue, but the Latinate word exceeds her vocabulary; she gropes toward it through the familiar flower-names 'honeysuckle' and 'honey-seed' (the twining vine and its seeds), which share a vague phonetic resemblance. 'Quell' (from Old English 'cwellan,' to kill) was archaic but not dead in Shakespeare's English; 'man-queller' and 'woman-queller' are Quickly's own inventions. The outburst captures her simultaneously furious, indignant, and linguistically overwhelmed.

The malapropism analysis — Quickly groping for 'homicidal'/'homicide' and landing on flower-names by phonetic proximity — is the mainstream scholarly reading, and 'quell' as an archaism for 'kill' is correctly sourced; the annotation does not over-claim intentional wordplay.

anchor_text: you scullion! you rampallian! you fustilarian! I'll tickle your catastrophe
summary: The Page hurls a volley of insults at the Hostess: a 'scullion' is a kitchen drudge (the lowest servant); a 'rampallian' is a scoundrel or ruffian; a 'fustilarian' is Shakespeare's apparent invention meaning something like a fat, fusty, worthless person. To 'tickle your catastrophe' is a euphemism for thrashing the Hostess's backside — 'catastrophe' meaning the hindquarters.
detail: The tiny Page has no physical threat to offer, so he tries to dominate through verbal violence. 'Scullion' (from Old French 'escouillon,' a mop) was a term of profound contempt. 'Rampallian' appears only here in Shakespeare and a few other Elizabethan texts; its origin is unclear, possibly from 'ramp' (a bold, licentious woman) plus a pejorative suffix. 'Fustilarian' appears nowhere else in English — it may be the Page's own compound from 'fusty' (musty, stale) or from 'fust' (rottenness). 'Catastrophe' means literally 'downturning' (Greek 'katastrophe') and was used as a term for the concluding part of a play, but here the Page employs it, almost certainly with a knowing smirk, for the Hostess's rear end.

The glosses for 'scullion' and 'rampallian' are defensible and well-sourced; 'fustilarian' as a Shakespearean hapax is correctly treated as probable nonce-coinage rather than a word with confirmed etymology, and 'tickle your catastrophe' as a euphemism for beating the backside is the standard reading supported by OED's transferred sense.

anchor_text: I will ride thee o' nights like the mare
summary: The 'mare' (or 'nightmare') was a demon in folklore believed to sit on the chest of a sleeping person, causing suffocating dreams — hence our word 'nightmare.' Mistress Quickly threatens to torment Falstaff as a night-hag does a sleeper. But 'ride' also carries a sexual sense, and Falstaff's reply plays back on exactly this: he cheerfully accepts the image but claims the problem will be finding enough ground to mount from, given his bulk.
detail: The Old English 'maere' (also 'mere,' 'mare') was a spirit — typically female — who oppressed sleeping victims by crouching on them, causing the sensation of suffocation and bad dreams. The 'night-mare' was a known folk terror throughout Europe. Falstaff's retort (TLN 638-639) — 'I think I am as like to ride the mare, if I have any vantage of ground to get up' — reverses the image: he will do the riding, but his great weight means he needs a leg up. 'Ride' as a sexual term and 'mare' as a slang word for a woman available for use are both attested in Elizabethan English (Williams, Glossary). The exchange is a characteristic Falstaff counter-punch: turning the Hostess's threat into a bawdy compliment to himself.

sources.citation: Gordon Williams, A Glossary of Shakespeare's Sexual Language (1997), s.v. 'ride,' 'mare.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 637

The nightmare-as-crushing-demon reading is well-founded etymologically, and Falstaff's rejoinder at TLN 638-639 ('if I have any vantage of ground to get up') demonstrably activates the sexual sense of 'ride,' confirming that both valences are present and the annotation is not projecting a double meaning — the text itself signals it.

anchor_text: upon a parcel-gilt goblet, sitting in my Dolphin-chamber, at the round table, by a sea-coal fire
summary: A 'parcel-gilt' cup is one that is only partly gilded — silver on the outside with gold on the inside (or gilded only at the rim and handle) — as opposed to fully gold. It was a middling-quality piece of plate, respectable but not grand. Mistress Quickly's precise inventory of the scene — named room, shape of table, type of fire — gives the false oath its comic legal weight.
detail: 'Parcel' in compounds means 'partial, partly' (from Old French 'parcelle,' Latin 'particula'). A 'parcel-gilt' or 'parcel-gold' object was standard in Elizabethan inventories of household plate; fully gilt was more expensive, and plain silver cheaper. 'Sea-coal' was coal brought by sea from Northumberland and Durham to London — as opposed to charcoal — and was the common domestic fuel by Shakespeare's day. The 'Dolphin-chamber' is a named room in the Boar's Head tavern; tavern rooms were commonly given names (the Dolphin, the Half-Moon) for identification. Quickly's loving specificity — the exact room, the round table, the kind of coal — parodies the formal precision of an oath sworn before a legal witness.

'Parcel-gilt' as partially gilded plate is exactly right as a period term of art in household inventories, 'sea-coal' as Northumbrian coal shipped to London is correct, and the annotation's point that Quickly's loving specificity parodies the precision of a sworn oath is a sound interpretive claim grounded in what the text does.

anchor_text: the one you may do with sterling money, and the other with current repentance
summary: The Lord Chief Justice draws a pointed parallel between money and morality using terms from currency: 'sterling' money is genuine, legally valid coin; 'current' repentance is sincere, acceptable — literally repentance that 'passes current' like good coin. Both words are monetary, applied to two different kinds of debt Falstaff owes the Hostess.
detail: 'Sterling' originally referred to coins of a standard English silver content and came to mean genuine, of full value. 'Current' in monetary usage meant coin or bills that were accepted in circulation — in good standing, not counterfeit or devalued (OED s.v. 'current,' adj. 7: 'Passing in ordinary circulation; in common use'). The Chief Justice's conceit maps financial debt (pay the money) onto moral debt (repay her honour), insisting that Falstaff owes on both accounts. The wordplay is characteristic of the play's sustained interest in credit, debt, and the gap between reputation and reality.

anchor_text: I will not undergo this sneap without reply
summary: A 'sneap' (also 'snape' or 'snap') is a sharp rebuke or a nipping check — the word comes from a root meaning to pinch or bite. Falstaff is refusing to accept the Lord Chief Justice's public correction without answering back.
detail: The word 'sneap' (from Old Norse 'sneypa,' to shame or check) was in use from the medieval period but had become archaic by the seventeenth century; it appears rarely in Shakespeare (also at Love's Labour's Lost 1.1, where Biron speaks of being 'sneaped with' the cold). The sense is of a sharp, stinging verbal reproof — less formal than a 'rebuke' and more personal than a 'censure.' Falstaff's resistance is characteristic: throughout the play he refuses the authority of anyone who challenges him, particularly the Chief Justice, though his justification — that 'honourable boldness' is being mistaken for 'impudent sauciness' — is transparently self-serving.

The gloss of 'sneap' as a sharp verbal rebuke and its Old Norse derivation are uncontroversial; the annotation correctly notes the word's archaic status by the seventeenth century and Falstaff's characteristic resistance to authority without over-reading his speech as heroic.

anchor_text: the story of the Prodigal, or the German hunting in water-work, is worth a thousand of these bed-hangings and these fly-bitten tapestries
summary: Falstaff dismisses the Hostess's tapestries — the woven hangings that decorated the walls of her rooms — and recommends cheaper 'water-work' (watercolor-painted cloth) showing the story of the Prodigal Son, the parable from Luke of the son who squanders his inheritance and returns home to be forgiven. The detail is darkly comic: the Prodigal's story — a son who drains his father's wealth in reckless living — mirrors exactly what Falstaff has done to the Hostess.
detail: The Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11-32, Geneva 1599) was one of the most common subjects for the cheap painted cloths that hung in tavern rooms and middle-class houses as inexpensive substitutes for woven tapestry; it was also a stock subject of actual tapestries. 'Water-work' refers to a kind of distemper or watercolor painting on cloth, much cheaper than wool tapestry. The 'German hunting' design was another conventional motif — woodland hunting scenes in the northern European manner. Falstaff's advice to sell the plate and replace expensive hangings with painted cloths is entirely self-serving: it gets him more cash now and leaves the Hostess worse furnished. The allusion to the Prodigal is a signature joke: the very emblem hanging on the tavern wall passes unnoticed judgment on what goes on beneath it.

sources.citation: Luke 15:11-32 (Geneva 1599): the parable of the Prodigal Son, including 'riotous living' at verse 13.

anchor_text: desire small beer
summary: 'Small beer' was the weakest, cheapest grade of ale -- a thin brew with very little alcohol, drunk by servants and the poor. Prince Hal treats his craving for it as a social embarrassment: a prince ought not to notice, let alone miss, so humble a drink.
detail: Beer was brewed in graduated strengths in Tudor England; 'small beer' (low-alcohol, second or third runnings of the mash) was standard household drink for servants, while 'double beer' and 'strong ale' were the beverages of the wealthy. For Hal to 'remember the poor creature, small beer' (TLN 742) signals the genuine affection for low company that runs through both Henry IV plays -- and that he self-mockingly diagnoses as a flaw in princely dignity.

anchor_text: engraffed to Falstaff
summary: 'Engraffed' (also spelled 'engrafted') means deeply joined or fixed, taken from the horticultural process of grafting a shoot onto a rootstock so the two grow together as one plant. Poins is saying that Hal has grown so attached to Falstaff that they have become virtually one organism.

anchor_text: I am a second brother and that I am a proper fellow of my hands
summary: A 'second brother' under Elizabethan primogeniture inherited nothing: the eldest son took the entire estate and title, leaving younger brothers to make their own way by soldiering, the law, or (like Poins) attaching themselves to a great lord. Poins half-ruefully acknowledges this as a built-in social disadvantage he cannot change. 'A proper fellow of my hands' means a capable, able-bodied man -- a competent fighter -- but one without the birth or money to stand on rank.
detail: Primogeniture (the rule that the eldest son inherits everything) was near-universal among the English landed gentry and aristocracy. It preserved estates intact but created a class of propertyless younger sons who often gravitated toward adventure, service, or dubious company -- exactly the Eastcheap world. The tension between birth-rank and personal ability runs through the scene: Poins can't help being a second son any more than he can help his face.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 784

Poins names his situation explicitly at TLN 784-785; the primogeniture context is historically accurate and the reading is mainstream.

anchor_text: this wen to be as familiar with me as my dog
summary: A 'wen' is a benign cyst or lump of fatty tissue growing just under the skin -- harmless but unsightly and hard to get rid of. Prince Hal's self-deprecating joke is that Falstaff is a growth attached to him: not dangerous, but not something a prince should publicly admit to. That he tolerates it as he tolerates his dog makes the indulgence all the stranger.

A 'wen' as a benign sebaceous cyst is precisely the right sense; Hal's self-deprecating comparison of Falstaff to a harmless but unsightly growth is straightforwardly supported by the text.

anchor_text: kin to the king; for they never prick their finger but they say
summary: Poins mocks the social climbers of his day who loudly claimed distant kinship with the royal family to bask in reflected prestige. The joke: anyone who pricks a finger in the king's presence immediately announces 'There's some of the king's blood spilt' -- meaning the same blood runs in their veins -- and then, asked how, produces the formulaic humble-brag 'I am the king's poor cousin.' Such vague claims of royal descent were both common and largely impossible to disprove.
detail: The Tudor period produced a great number of people who could trace a plausible, if distant, connection to Edward III's many descendants, and claiming royal blood was a useful social currency. The joke also works because Falstaff, in his letter, styles himself 'Sir John Falstaff, knight' with full ceremony every time he uses his own name -- the same self-important insistence on titles that marks the fake cousins.

The mock-kinship joke is clearly set up at TLN 819-825, and the extension to Falstaff's own title-insistence as the same pattern of self-important pretension is a reasonable and defensible reading.

anchor_text: fetch it from Japhet
summary: Japheth was one of Noah's three sons and, in the biblical tradition that Shakespeare's audience learned in church, the ancestor of all European peoples. Prince Hal is mocking those who claim distant royal kinship: if pressed hard enough, they will trace their blood all the way back to Japheth -- the ultimate ancestor of every person in Europe -- so the claim proves nothing at all.
detail: Genesis 10:2-5 (Geneva 1599) lists Japheth's sons as the progenitors of the nations of Europe and Asia Minor; he was universally cited as the forefather of the Europeans. The joke's logic is reductio ad absurdum: if you want a pedigree broad enough to guarantee a shared ancestor with the king, Japheth is the farthest you can go -- at which point the claim is universal and meaningless.

anchor_text: imitate the honourable Romans in brevity
summary: Roman letter-writing set the standard for formal correspondence in Tudor England, with Cicero's letters most often cited as the model; brevity and compression were praised as a Roman virtue. Falstaff's claim to 'imitate the honourable Romans in brevity' is undercut at once by the letter's rambling style, and Poins skewers it: the only brevity Falstaff has is 'brevity in breath, short-winded' -- he is too fat to breathe, let alone write crisply.
detail: Cicero's Epistulae ad Atticum and Epistulae ad Familiares were read and imitated in Tudor grammar schools as models of Latinity; the formula 'si vales, bene est' (if you are well, good) was a recognized letter-opening. Falstaff's 'I commend me to thee, I commend thee, and I leave thee' parodies exactly these brief, formulaic Latin salutations -- but his letter then wanders into gossip about Poins and Nell, demolishing any claim to Roman concision.

sources.name: Cicero, Epistulae ad Atticum

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 832
