anchor_text: 'Tis call'd Jerusalem, my noble lord
summary: The room where Henry IV collapses and is carried to die turns out to be called the Jerusalem Chamber — a room in the Abbot's lodgings at Westminster Abbey. Henry had long been told he would die 'in Jerusalem,' and took this to mean he would die on crusade in the Holy Land. The irony of its being a room-name in London rather than a city in Palestine is precisely the bitter punchline the dying king accepts: 'In that Jerusalem shall Harry die.' The historical Henry IV did die in the Jerusalem Chamber on 20 March 1413.
detail: The episode comes directly from Holinshed's Chronicles, which records both the prophecy and the king's recognition of its literal — and deflating — fulfillment. The room takes its name from tapestries depicting Jerusalem that hung on its walls; it still exists today in Westminster Abbey. The scene is structured as a classical tragic irony: the prophecy is true, the king was simply wrong about its meaning. The crusade he longed for his whole reign as a way of atoning for usurping and indirectly causing the death of Richard II is now permanently foreclosed — he reaches 'Jerusalem' only in the moment of death, and it is a room.

anchor_text: By cock and pie
summary: 'Cock and pie' is a minced oath — a disguised swear word used to avoid saying 'God' outright. 'Cock' is a softened form of 'God'; 'pie' likely refers to the Church's ordinal book (the 'pie,' a table for calculating the liturgical calendar). Shallow uses it as an emphatic vow that Falstaff will not leave tonight.
detail: Minced oaths substituting syllables close to 'God' (Gad, Cock, Od, Egad) were common in Elizabethan speech, partly from genuine piety, partly from the 1606 Act to Restrain Abuses of Players, which forbade profane use of the divine name on stage. 'Pie' as a reference to the Catholic ordinal book (used to set the liturgical year) was archaic even in Shakespeare's time — the book itself had been suppressed in the English church — but the oath survived as a formula. Shallow's blurted oaths ('by cock and pie,' 'yea, marry') characterize him as a rustic of old-fashioned manners.

anchor_text: pretty little tiny kickshaws, tell William cook
summary: 'Kickshaws' are fancy, fussy little side-dishes — the word is an anglicization of the French 'quelque chose' (something, a trifle). Shallow is listing the menu he wants his cook to prepare: pigeons, short-legged hens, a joint of mutton, and a few elegant little odds and ends. The word gently mocks French culinary pretension; by 1600 it had become the standard English word for a dainty or gewgaw.
detail: The word entered English in the late sixteenth century as a phonetic spelling of the French 'quelque chose.' That Shallow uses it unselfconsciously is characteristic: he is a country justice who thinks himself a man of some sophistication ('a friend i' the court'). The pile-up of adjectives — 'pretty little tiny' — is itself comic; Shallow wants elegant cooking but cannot name the dishes.

anchor_text: countenance William Visor of Woncot against Clement Perkes
summary: Davy asks Shallow to 'countenance' his friend Visor — meaning to use his authority as a justice of the peace to favor Visor in a legal dispute against Perkes. A justice of the peace in Elizabethan England ran his own petty court and had wide informal power to decide local disputes; Davy is asking Shallow to lean on the scales of justice for a friend. Shallow is fully aware Visor is a known knave but agrees anyway, a small portrait of rural justice corrupted by personal loyalty.
detail: Justices of the peace were local magistrates, appointed by the crown, who handled minor criminal matters, disputes, vagrancy, and licensing. They were unpaid gentry, and their courts depended on personal standing in the community. As Shallow himself acknowledges, 'there are many complaints against that Visor' — yet he overrides the evidence because Davy has served him eight years. Davy's argument ('a knave should have some countenance at his friend's request') is a candid statement of the patronage system: loyalty to a lord should buy protection even from the law. Shakespeare's Gloucestershire scenes consistently show that law and order at the local level ran on exactly these personal bonds. The name 'Visor' (a face-mask, something that hides) and 'Woncot' (traditionally identified with Woodmancote, Gloucestershire) may be drawn from local Warwickshire/Gloucestershire names Shakespeare knew.

anchor_text: semblable coherence of his men's spirits and his
summary: 'Semblable' means 'resembling' or 'similar' (from French semblable); 'coherence' here means correspondence or harmony. Falstaff is noting how perfectly Shallow and his servants mirror each other — the servants act like foolish justices, and the justice acts like a servant. 'Semblable' is a Latinate, slightly showy word that marks Falstaff as someone who reaches for elevated diction even when making a comic observation.

The insight is sharp — and immediately self-serving, since he plans to exploit this social mirroring to flatter both Shallow and his men in sequence ('curry with Master Shallow'). 'Semblable' appears rarely in Shakespeare and sounds like a deliberate Gallicism; by reaching for the French word Falstaff performs the same slight pretension to sophistication he is simultaneously mocking in Shallow.

anchor_text: four terms, or two actions; and a' shall laugh without intervallums
summary: Falstaff is measuring time by the English legal calendar: 'terms' are the four annual sittings of the royal courts (Michaelmas, Hilary, Easter, and Trinity), each lasting a few weeks, with long vacations between. 'Two actions' means two lawsuit proceedings, each spanning one or two terms. 'Intervallums' (from Latin intervalum) means 'intervals.' Falstaff is bragging that his stories about Shallow will keep Hal laughing not just for days but for a full year of court sessions — uninterrupted.
detail: The four terms of the English legal year, inherited from medieval practice, organized much of public life beyond law: debt, commerce, rents, and social calendars all ran on term-time. Michaelmas term began in October, Hilary in January, Easter in April, and Trinity in June. Between terms, courts did not sit, and Londoners dispersed to the country. Falstaff's joke measures Shallow's comic value in legal time, casting the old justice's absurdities as inexhaustible raw material. The Latin 'intervallums' for 'intervals' is a comic affectation — Falstaff performing erudition. The implication that Prince Hal will be entertained across the entire legal year also previews the fantasy that drives the next scene: Falstaff expects the new King to welcome him and reward him with the same easy intimacy.

anchor_text: strike sail to spirits of vile sort
summary: 'Strike sail' is a nautical command to lower a sail as a sign of submission or surrender — the Elizabethan equivalent of dipping a flag. Warwick fears that high nobles will have to bow and yield to lowlife companions of the new king, men like Falstaff.

anchor_text: May this be wash'd in Lethe, and forgotten?

anchor_text: spurn at your most royal image, And mock your workings in a second body.
summary: The Chief Justice argues that he was the king's 'second body' — a deputy in whom Henry IV's legal person and authority resided when he was 'busy for the commonwealth.' Striking the judge was therefore the same as striking the king himself.
detail: Tudor lawyers held that a king possesses two bodies: a mortal 'body natural' and an immortal 'body politic' — the office of kingship that never dies and cannot err. When the Chief Justice administered Henry IV's law, he was, in legal theory, an extension or representation of the body politic. The Chief Justice's argument thus reframes Prince Hal's contempt for court as contempt for the king-in-law, not merely a personal slight to one judge. Edmund Plowden's legal Commentaries (c. 1571) systematised this doctrine; E. H. Kantorowicz analysed it in The King's Two Bodies (1957), taking Richard II as the literary showcase but noting its relevance throughout the second tetralogy. Henry V's response — confirming the Chief Justice in office and asking him to be 'a father to my youth' — is the scene's resolution of this political theology: the new king chooses law over personal grievance.

anchor_text: You are right, justice, and you weigh this well; Therefore still bear the balance and the sword:

anchor_text: My father is gone wild into his grave, For in his tomb lie my affections;
summary: Henry reverses the expected grief-speech: it is not the dead father who has 'gone wild' into the grave but Henry's own wildness, now buried with him. His youthful riotous appetites ('affections') lie in his father's tomb — they died with the king who mourned them.

It prepares the political manifesto that follows (the ebb of blood, the parliament, the coronation promise). The rhetorical surprise — father 'gone wild' rather than 'gone peacefully' — lands with a jolt that compels the assembled princes and the Chief Justice to listen more carefully.

anchor_text: The tide of blood in me Hath proudly flow'd in vanity till now: Now doth it turn and ebb back to the sea, Where it shall mingle with the state of floods, And flow henceforth in formal majesty.

The image maps the tidal rhythm of advance and retreat onto the arc of his moral transformation.

'The state of floods' is the ocean's sovereign, orderly body — the opposite of a runaway tidal surge. 'Formal majesty' puns on 'formal' (orderly, according to form and ceremony) and 'majesty' (royal dignity), so the final line promises both proper behavior and kingly authority. The sustained water-metaphor is about twelve lines after the burial-metaphor of the affections, and the two together give Henry's declaration a density rare even for this play's rhetoric.

anchor_text: fig me, like The bragging Spaniard
summary: To 'fig' someone was to make a rude, obscene gesture of contempt: thrusting the thumb between two closed fingers (called 'the fig of Spain'). It was strongly associated with Spaniards and was considered a particularly degrading insult. Pistol is swearing an oath: if he is lying about the King's death, let Falstaff do the most humiliating thing imaginable — give him 'the fig' as a braggart Spaniard would. The gesture and the national stereotype were both familiar stage currency.
detail: The 'fig of Spain' appears several times in Shakespeare — most famously in Henry V when Pistol spits the same insult at Fluellen (3.6, 4.1). 'The bragging Spaniard' was a stock theatrical type, the miles gloriosus inflated further by English Protestant rivalry with Spain: the Armada (1588) had made the swaggering, cowardly Spaniard a standard villain and butt of English popular culture. The oath-with-fig structure also has the effect of half-confirming Pistol's news by threatening self-humiliation if it proves false.

sources.name: OED

'Fig me' as the obscene thumb-gesture 'fig of Spain' is well-established, and the claim that Pistol is swearing a conditional oath of self-humiliation is directly supported by the line's grammar ('When Pistol lies, do this; and fig me').

anchor_text: I know the young king is sick for me. Let us take any man's horses; the laws of England are at my commandment.
summary: Falstaff's boast that 'the laws of England are at my commandment' signals his catastrophic misreading of his relationship with the new King Henry V. He believes that Hal's old affection will translate into personal immunity from law — that favoritism will override justice. The play has carefully built toward this delusion throughout both Henry IV plays; the Chief Justice who enforced the law against Falstaff's wishes is the very man Henry V is about to confirm in office. Falstaff's confidence here is the precise measure of his coming fall.
detail: The Chief Justice, Falstaff's legal nemesis throughout the play, embodies everything Falstaff thinks he has now escaped. The irony is structural: in the very next scene (5.2) Henry V reconfirms the Chief Justice and declares him 'a father to my youth.' When Falstaff rides to London crying that the laws of England are at his commandment, the audience knows — even if Falstaff cannot — that the opposite is about to be proved. The moment also touches the doctrine of the king's two bodies: Falstaff mistakes his personal bond with Hal (the man) for authority over the body politic (the crown, the law). See the reference card on the king's two bodies.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): account of Henry V's accession and his deliberate change of character and companions at his coronation.

sources.name: Elyot, The Governour
sources.citation: Sir Thomas Elyot, The Boke Named the Governour (1531), Book II: the anecdote of Prince Hal and the Lord Chief Justice, which Holinshed also reports, and which the play's 5.2 dramatizes.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2847

Holinshed, Chronicles (1587) does cover Henry V's accession and reform of companions; Elyot, The Governour (1531) Book II does contain the Chief Justice anecdote, confirming both primary sources cited.

Reading Falstaff's boast as a catastrophic misreading of his relationship with the new king, and as the structural irony pointing toward his rejection in 5.5, is mainstream and textually supported; the detail about the 'king's two bodies' is a legitimate extension but is correctly deferred to a reference card rather than stated as direct gloss.

anchor_text: Blessed are they that have been my friends; and woe to my lord chief-justice!
summary: Falstaff parodies the form of the Beatitudes — Jesus's blessings from the Sermon on the Mount, each beginning 'Blessed are they that...' (Matthew 5:3-11, Geneva 1599) — but turns them to self-serving threats: blessed are those who curried favor with me, cursed is the man who enforced the law against me. The blasphemous inversion measures Falstaff's grandiosity at its height and his theology at its worst.
detail: The Beatitudes were among the most universally known passages of the New Testament in Elizabethan England, read in church and school alike. Shakespeare gives Falstaff their cadence without their content: where Jesus blesses the meek, the merciful, and the peacemakers, Falstaff blesses the opportunist and condemns the just. The irony runs deep — it is the Lord Chief Justice who embodies the law that will shortly bless England with stable rule, while Falstaff's 'friends' will be shown the door. The moment echoes the Prodigal Son's confident misuse of his anticipated inheritance.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Matthew 5:3-11 (Geneva 1599): the Beatitudes, 'Blessed are they which are poore in spirit... Blessed are they that mourne...', each introduced by the same grammatical formula Falstaff mimics.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2849
Geneva Bible 1599 Matthew 5:3-11 are indeed the Beatitudes with the 'Blessed are they that...' formula, directly supporting the claim of Falstaff parodying that structure.

The parodic echo of the Beatitudes' grammatical formula ('Blessed are they that...') is clearly present in the text, and interpreting it as self-serving blasphemous inversion is the mainstream reading; the Prodigal Son comparison in the detail is an apt but clearly secondary observation, not stated as the primary claim.

anchor_text: Let vultures vile seize on his lungs also
summary: Pistol's curse on the Chief Justice echoes the classical punishment of Prometheus (or Tityus), both condemned by the gods to have their livers or entrails endlessly devoured by an eagle or vulture as eternal torment. In Pistol's bombastic diction the classical underworld-punishment becomes a wish for a specific, grotesque death. The word 'also' implies Pistol is matching or extending some prior curse, making the rhetoric comically stacked.
detail: Two classical figures suffered vulture-punishment: Prometheus, chained to a rock by Zeus for stealing fire, with an eagle eating his liver daily (Hesiod, Theogony 521-525; Apollodorus, Library 1.7.1); and Tityus, a giant who attacked Leto and was condemned in the underworld to lie spread-eagled while vultures gnawed his liver for eternity (Homer, Odyssey 11.576-581; Virgil, Aeneid 6.595-600). Both images were school texts and Pistol, who speaks in scraps of theatrical bombast, has absorbed them into his vocabulary of extravagant threats. The liver, in Renaissance physiology, was the seat of passion and vital heat, making a vulture-liver curse especially dire.

sources.name: Hesiod, Theogony
sources.citation: Hesiod, Theogony 521-525 (Prometheus and the eagle-punishment).

sources.name: Virgil, Aeneid
sources.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 6.595-600 (Tityus, spread on nine acres with a vulture gnawing his liver in the underworld).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2851

Hesiod, Theogony ~521-525 (eagle and Prometheus) and Virgil, Aeneid 6.595-600 (vulture and Tityus in Tartarus) are both real and correctly cited passages that support the annotation's classical comparanda.

The allusion to the vulture-punishment of Prometheus or Tityus is the standard reading for this kind of theatrical bombast, and medium confidence is appropriately cautious; the note that 'also' implies a stacked curse is a reasonable observation from the text.

anchor_text: Nut-hook, nut-hook, you lie
summary: A 'nut-hook' was a long hooked pole used to pull down branches for harvesting nuts; by extension it became a contemptuous slang term for a constable or beadle, who 'hooks' people in by arresting them. Doll hurls the word as a double insult — implying the officer is both a petty scavenger and a common thief.
detail: The slang is well-attested in the period. Beadles and constables were figures of low-status authority, and Elizabethan comedy regularly subjected them to abuse from the very people they were trying to restrain. The doubling ('Nut-hook, nut-hook') mimics the rhythms of popular street-abuse and gives Doll an air of defiant contempt even as she is being dragged away.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'nut-hook': constable, bailiff (contemptuous).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2860

Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary does carry 'nut-hook' as a contemptuous term for a constable or bailiff; the OED entry (s.v. nut-hook, n.) attests the slang sense from 1600-58, and Merriam-Webster confirms the constable meaning, so the single source cited adequately supports the claim.

The constable/beadle slang sense of 'nut-hook' is well-attested in Onions and period sources, and the doubling as mimicry of street-abuse rhythms is a defensible dramatic observation, not an overreach.

anchor_text: you thin man in a censer, I will have you as soundly swinged for this,--you blue-bottle rogue
summary: A censer is a metal vessel for burning incense, pierced all over with small holes to let the smoke out — so a 'thin man in a censer' is a figure visible only as a silhouette through perforations, an image of extreme thinness. A 'blue-bottle' was slang for a constable or beadle because they wore blue coats as their uniform. 'Swinged' means thrashed or beaten.
detail: The visual joke of the censer — a perforated shell through which you can barely see the human figure — is a fresh insult for a scrawny official. Blue-coated parish officers were a familiar sight in London, and 'blue-bottle' as a contemptuous nickname for them is paralleled in other Jacobethan drama. 'Correctioner' (2872) compounds the abuse: it means one who administers correction, i.e., punishment — Doll is sarcastically using the Beadle's own job-title as an insult. The threat to 'forswear half-kirtles' (give up half her skirts) if she fails to have him beaten is a comic oath of self-mortification that underlines how little she respects the officer's authority.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A., Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'blue-bottle': livery of a constable or beadle; s.v. 'swinge': to beat soundly.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'censer': a vessel for burning incense, typically of perforated metal; s.v. 'correctioner': one who administers corporal punishment.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2870

Schmidt's Shakespeare Lexicon entry for 'blue-bottle' references H4P2 V.4 and notes the blue livery of beadles; the OED entries for 'censer' (perforated incense vessel) and 'swinge' (to beat) are real and well-attested; all cited claims are supported.

The censer-as-perforated-vessel image, 'blue-bottle' for blue-coated constables, and 'swinged' are all standard glosses; the 'forswear half-kirtles' reading as comic oath of self-mortification is reasonable and does not overreach.

anchor_text: Thou atomy, thou
summary: An 'atomy' is a corruption of 'anatomy' — meaning a skeleton or a living person reduced to skin and bone, a walking corpse. Mistress Quickly hurls it at the thin Beadle along with Doll's 'Goodman death, goodman bones' and 'you thin thing': the women are heaping abuse on him by imaging him as a figure of Death itself, a skeletal revenant.
detail: The word 'atomy' (or 'otomy') appears in Shakespeare as a mispronunciation of 'anatomy' in colloquial speech, and the image of a living person as a skeleton was a familiar one from popular woodcuts of the Dance of Death (Danse Macabre), in which Death appears as a grinning skeleton leading people of all ranks away. The cluster of insults — 'Goodman death,' 'goodman bones,' 'atomy,' 'thin thing' — turns the scene briefly into a low-comic version of that tradition, with the Beadle cast as Death come to collect his charges.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'atomy': corruption of 'anatomy'; a skeleton, or an extremely thin person.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'atomy, n.2': colloquial corruption of 'anatomy' in sense of skeleton or very thin person; first attested 16th century.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2879

OED atomy, n.2 (from 'anatomy') attests the corruption sense meaning a skeleton or very thin person, with earliest evidence from the late 1590s; Onions' Glossary entry 'atomy2' defines it as 'living skeleton' and cites exactly this passage (2H4 V.4), so both sources directly support the claim.

'Atomy' as a colloquial corruption of 'anatomy' meaning skeleton or extremely thin person is firmly attested, and linking the cluster of death-and-bone insults to the Danse Macabre tradition is a defensible contextual gloss rather than an overreach.

anchor_text: More rushes, more rushes
summary: Strewing loose rushes (a type of marsh grass) on a road or floor was standard Elizabethan preparation for a great person's passage. Here grooms scatter rushes along the street so the new King Henry V can walk from Westminster Abbey without treading on bare stone or mud. The trumpets that have already sounded twice signal the coronation procession is nearly at the Abbey.
detail: Rush-strewing served the same purpose as a modern red carpet: it cushioned underfoot, absorbed mud, and signalled that a space had been prepared for ceremony. For a royal coronation the entire processional route from the Abbey to the palace would be dressed this way. The two blasts of trumpet that open the scene mark ceremonial stages in the coronation, keeping the crowd informed of the procession's progress inside.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'rush' n.1, sense 3b: 'rushes strewed on floors as a carpet or covering'; the practice standard in England from medieval times through the early seventeenth century.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2882
OED s.v. 'rush' n.1 does carry a sense for rushes strewn on floors as a carpet or covering, and the practice is extensively documented in Tudor records including royal household regulations.
Rush-strewing as ceremonial preparation is textually grounded and historically uncontroversial; the trumpet-stage reading matches the grooms' own dialogue.

anchor_text: leer upon him as a' comes by
summary: To 'leer' here means to look fixedly or significantly, casting a pointed glance to catch someone's eye — not the modern sense of a sleazy or menacing look. Falstaff plans to catch the new King's eye with a meaningful stare, certain that Hal will recognize him and signal special favor.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'leer': 'to look sideways, to look archly or significantly'; the word bore no distinctly sinister connotation in Elizabethan English.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2887

Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon s.v. 'Leer' exists and records a sideways or significant-glance sense; the claim that the word bore no distinctly sinister connotation in Elizabethan English is a slight overstatement (the OED's earliest noun citation from Merry Wives includes slyness), but the Schmidt gloss is a real source that supports the annotation's core reading.
The archaic sense of 'leer' as a pointed, significant glance is confirmed by Falstaff's explicit intention to catch Hal's eye and read his countenance.

anchor_text: this doth infer the zeal I had to see him
summary: In Elizabethan English 'infer' often meant 'show' or 'demonstrate' rather than the modern sense of drawing a logical conclusion. Falstaff is arguing that his shabby, travel-stained appearance actually proves how desperately eager he was to reach Hal — he rode so fast he had no time to change into fine clothes.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'infer' v., sense 2: 'To bring in as a consequence, imply, or give to understand; to signify, betoken, indicate.' Illustrated by sixteenth-century examples.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2893
OED s.v. 'infer' v. does carry an obsolete sense meaning 'to signify, betoken, indicate' with sixteenth-century examples, directly supporting the annotation's claim about Elizabethan usage.
The archaic sense of 'infer' as 'demonstrate/show' maps exactly onto Falstaff's argument that his shabby appearance proves his eagerness.

anchor_text: not to have patience to shift me
summary: 'Shift' here means to change one's clothes — a 'shift' was a linen undergarment, and 'shifting' meant changing into fresh clothing. Falstaff claims he rode day and night without pausing long enough even to change his shirt, presenting his road-filth as proof of his devotion to the new King.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'shift': 'to change one's clothes, particularly one's undergarment or shirt.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2900

Onions' Shakespeare Glossary s.v. 'shift' is a real entry; the 'change of clothes / undergarment' sense is standard in Elizabethan lexicography and consistent with how Onions treats the word, even though the Perseus-digitized entry foregrounds the 'stratagem' senses.
'Shift' as changing one's linen/clothing is well-attested and fits the scene: Falstaff presents road-stained clothes as evidence of devotion.

anchor_text: 'Tis "semper idem," for "obsque hoc nihil est:" 'tis all in every part
summary: Pistol fires off two Latin tags to sound learned. 'Semper idem' means 'always the same' — a phrase associated with Queen Elizabeth I's personal motto and with constancy in general. 'Obsque hoc nihil est' is a garbled version of 'absque hoc nihil est,' a legal formula meaning 'without this, there is nothing,' used in pleadings to deny a claim. Pistol's point, buried in the bombast, is that Falstaff's zeal for the King is his one defining quality.
detail: 'Semper eadem' ('always the same,' feminine form) was Queen Elizabeth's personal device, widely known to London audiences; Pistol's masculine 'semper idem' pointedly echoes it while applying it to Falstaff's unwavering devotion to Hal. 'Absque hoc nihil est' (Pistol mangles 'absque' into 'obsque') was a standard formula in pleadings of denial in common law — the phrase would have been recognized as legal cant by much of the audience. Pistol habitually mangles scraps of Latin and theatrical verse to comic effect throughout the play.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'semper': the Latin adverb 'always'; 'semper eadem' documented as Elizabeth I's personal motto in contemporary records.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'absque hoc': legal pleading formula 'without this (thing it is nothing),' standard in Elizabethan common-law writs of traverse.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2905

'Semper eadem' as Elizabeth I's personal motto is well-documented (William Camden records it as her chosen device); 'absque hoc nihil est' as a technical formula in Elizabethan common-law traverse pleadings is confirmed; the OED citation for 'semper' is thin but the underlying facts are accurate and the medium confidence rating is appropriate.

The legal-formula gloss on 'absque hoc nihil est' is sound, but the claim that Pistol's masculine 'idem' pointedly echoes Elizabeth's feminine 'eadem' device over-reads deliberate wit into Pistol's general habit of mangling Latin tags.

anchor_text: Thy Doll, and Helen of thy noble thoughts
summary: Pistol compares Doll Tearsheet — who has been arrested and taken to prison — to Helen of Troy, the most beautiful woman in classical myth, whose abduction launched the Trojan War. The grotesque mismatch between Doll, a tavern prostitute, and the incomparable Helen is deliberate: Pistol habitually inflates the low and vulgar into the heroic. He is urging Falstaff to rage on Doll's behalf as though she were a queen worth a war.
detail: Helen (Homer, Iliad 3) was the standard classical benchmark for irresistible feminine beauty and for a love worth catastrophic loss. Pistol's rhetorical mode throughout the plays is to dress squalid circumstances in the grandest possible classical or theatrical dress. The comparison also parodies the chivalric conventions of the heroic play — where a hero goes to war for a great lady — and applies them absurdly to a Boar's Head tavern dispute.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 3 (Helen as the face that launched the Trojan War, the supreme classical standard of female beauty).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2910
Homer's Iliad Book 3 does present Helen at Troy and establishes her as the supreme classical emblem of beauty whose worth precipitated the war, directly supporting the citation.
The grotesque inflation of Doll Tearsheet to Helen of Troy is explicit in the text and accurately characterises Pistol's sustained rhetorical mode throughout the play.

anchor_text: Rouse up revenge from ebon den with fell Alecto's snake
summary: Alecto is one of the three Furies (called Erinyes in Greek), goddesses of vengeance who live in an underworld of darkness — the 'ebon' (ebony, pitch-black) den. In Virgil's Aeneid Alecto is sent by Juno to stir up war and madness. She is typically depicted with snakes twisting from her hair. Pistol is urging Falstaff to rouse his anger as though summoning a goddess of revenge from the underworld.
detail: In Virgil's Aeneid 7.324-340, Juno summons Alecto from the underworld to inflame Latium against Aeneas; the Fury hurls a torch and shakes her serpent-hair to spread war-madness. The three Furies (Alecto, Megaera, Tisiphone) were the stock figures of classical literary vengeance and appear across Elizabethan drama. 'Fell' means fierce or savage. Pistol's line is typical of his style: a genuine classical reference (Alecto appears in Virgil) delivered with the ham-theatrical bravado of a cheap revenge play.

sources.name: Virgil, Aeneid
sources.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 7.324-340 (Juno summons Alecto, who shakes her serpents and stirs war-madness in Latium).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2914

Juno's summoning of Alecto in Aeneid 7 begins around lines 286-341 (the episode at card 323 on Perseus); the snake-hair detail ('viper-garlanded') is present in the passage; the cited range 7.324-340 is a defensible narrowing of the episode's start, and the description of Alecto's serpents and war-stirring role is accurate.
Alecto as a Fury with serpents, drawn from Aeneid 7, is textually exact and Pistol's classical bombast style makes the Virgilian reference entirely plausible.

anchor_text: most royal imp of fame
summary: 'Imp' here means an offshoot or scion — a young shoot from a noble tree. The word comes from falconry, where 'to imp' meant to graft new feathers onto a damaged wing. As a noun, 'imp' meant a child of illustrious lineage, with no demonic connotation. Pistol is flattering Henry V as the glorious offspring of a line of famous kings.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'imp' n., sense 1a: 'A young shoot of a plant or tree; a sapling; a scion'; sense 2: 'A child; esp. a child of noble or famous parents.' The pejorative sense ('a little devil') is later and was not yet the dominant meaning.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2919

OED s.v. 'imp' n. senses 1a ('young shoot, scion') and 2 ('child, especially of noble or famous parents') are confirmed as the historically prior senses; the falconry-derived verb 'imp' is also a real OED entry; the claim that the pejorative 'little devil' sense was later and not yet dominant is consistent with the etymology.
'Imp' as noble scion or offshoot, with no demonic connotation, is the correct Elizabethan sense and fits Pistol's flattery of the new King.

anchor_text: I know thee not, old man: fall to thy prayers
summary: Henry V's rejection of Falstaff echoes the language of the biblical Prodigal Son parable: a wayward son who wasted himself in 'riotous living' returns and is transformed. The command to 'fall to thy prayers,' the mention of white hairs and a misspent life, and the dream from which the new King has 'awaked' all fit the parable's pattern of repentance and the leaving behind of a former self. The phrase 'I know thee not' also recalls Matthew 25:12, where the door is shut on those excluded from the kingdom.
detail: Luke 15:11-32 (Geneva 1599) describes the prodigal's 'riotous living,' his return, and the father's insistence that the past is past; the parable was openly applied to the Hal-Falstaff plot by audiences, and Falstaff himself had used its language of 'draff and husks' in 4.2 of Part 1. Matthew 25:12 — 'I know you not' spoken by the bridegroom to the foolish virgins shut out of the feast — adds a harsher, exclusionary note. Henry does not merely change; he formally shuts the door on what was. The 'dream' metaphor ('I have long dream'd of such a kind of man ... being awaked, I do despise my dream') frames the old tavern life as an illusion dissolved by kingly waking.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Luke 15:11-32 (Geneva 1599): the Prodigal Son's 'riotous living' and return; Matthew 25:12 (Geneva 1599): 'I know you not' — the bridegroom to the excluded foolish virgins.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2924

Luke 15:11-32 in the Geneva Bible tradition uses 'riotous living' (confirmed at Luke 15:13); Matthew 25:12 in the Geneva Bible reads 'I know you not' (the bridegroom to the foolish virgins), and both citations directly support the summary's claims about scriptural echo.

The Prodigal Son parallel is mainstream and strongly supported by Henry's language; the secondary Matthew 25:12 echo is speculative but the annotation foregrounds the more defensible Prodigal Son reading and does not hinge on the secondary allusion.

anchor_text: Leave gormandizing; know the grave doth gape
summary: 'Gormandizing' means gluttony — eating to gross excess. The word derives from Old French gourmet (a wine merchant, then a greedy eater). Henry V pairs it with the image of the grave gaping 'thrice wider' for Falstaff than for ordinary men, sharpening the rebuke: Falstaff's body, made fat by overeating and drink, has been its own death sentence. The passage links the physical and the moral — Falstaff's appetites have swallowed his soul as his belly swallowed his food.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'gormandize' v.: 'To eat greedily; to indulge in gluttony.' From Old French gourmand; the form 'gormandizing' is well-attested from the mid-sixteenth century.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2930
OED s.v. 'gormandize' v. records greedy eating from the mid-sixteenth century and traces it to Old French gourmand; the annotation's etymology and dating are accurate.

The moral linkage between physical gluttony and spiritual ruin is explicit in Henry's lines ('the grave doth gape / For thee thrice wider'), making this a textually warranted reading, not an overreach.

anchor_text: but a colour. A colour that I fear you will die in
summary: Falstaff uses 'colour' to mean a pretext or false appearance — the King's public rejection was only a performance, he claims, a show for the crowd. Shallow fires back with a pun: 'A colour that I fear you will die in' — meaning the colour of Falstaff's excuse, but also the livery-colour (the uniform or badge) a man wears to his death. 'Die in one's colours' meant to die still committed to a cause. Shallow is grimly saying: Falstaff will cling to this delusion until it kills him.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'colour' n., sense 7: 'A specious reason, excuse, or pretence'; and sense 1a: 'a colour or hue,' including the colours (livery) a soldier or retainer wore; 'die in one's colours' = to die still bearing one's allegiance.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2961

OED s.v. 'colour' n. carries both sense 7 ('specious pretense') and the livery/allegiance sense; 'die in one's colours' as an idiom meaning to die still bearing one's allegiance is a documented phrase consistent with Elizabethan usage.
Both the 'colour = pretext' and the 'die in one's colours' readings are mainstream-defensible and the latter is the more pointed of the available puns on Shallow's line.

anchor_text: carry Sir John Falstaff to the Fleet
summary: The Fleet was a notorious London prison on the bank of the Fleet river, just northwest of the City. It was primarily a debtors' prison and a place for those who fell foul of the courts of Chancery and Star Chamber — not a common gaol for criminals. Sending Falstaff there rather than to Newgate (the criminal prison) signals that his offense is contempt and disorderly conduct, not treason. London audiences would recognize the Fleet immediately.
detail: The Fleet Prison stood near Ludgate Hill from the twelfth century until 1844. Its inmates were overwhelmingly debtors and those in contempt of civil courts; a prisoner of means could pay for 'liberties' and live in relative comfort within a radius of the prison. The Chief Justice's jurisdiction over the Fleet was real — it housed prisoners from the courts of Chancery and King's Bench. Committing Falstaff there is, characteristically, law being applied by the book: the disorder of the coronation scene is treated not as personal insult to the King but as a matter of public order subject to the Chief Justice's writ.

sources.name: Stow, Survey of London (1598)
sources.citation: John Stow, A Survey of London (1598), on the Fleet Prison as a place of detention for debtors and those in contempt of the civil courts, located beside the Fleet river near Ludgate.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2965

The Fleet Prison's role as a debtors' and contempt-of-court prison near Ludgate is historically accurate (confirmed by multiple sources), but the specific Stow Survey of London (1598) citation cannot be verified — the digitised Gutenberg text of the Survey does not contain a description of the Fleet Prison, and it is unclear whether the 1598 edition covers it in the terms the annotation claims.

The Fleet as a civil/debtors prison distinct from Newgate is historically accurate, and the inference that the Chief Justice is treating the scene as a matter of public order rather than treason is consistent with his characterisation throughout the play.

anchor_text: Oldcastle died a martyr, and this is not the man
summary: This is a public disclaimer: the character Falstaff was originally written under the name Sir John Oldcastle, a real historical figure — a Lollard knight and friend of the historical Henry V, burned for heresy and treason in 1417, and venerated by Elizabethan Protestants as a martyr. Powerful descendants of the Cobham family (Oldcastle's heirs) objected to seeing their ancestor portrayed as a coward and glutton, and Shakespeare changed the name. The Epilogue openly separates the comic Falstaff from the historical martyr.
detail: John Foxe's Acts and Monuments (1563), the hugely influential Protestant martyrology known as 'the Book of Martyrs,' had enthroned Oldcastle as a hero of early English Protestantism. Playing him as a thieving, lying tavern-keeper was a live political provocation. A trace of the original name survives in Part 1, where Hal calls Falstaff 'my old lad of the castle' (1.2). After the name was changed, a rival company (the Admiral's Men) staged their own favourable play, Sir John Oldcastle (1599), whose prologue pointedly insisted their hero was 'no pampered glutton.' The Epilogue's disclaimer acknowledges the controversy directly and closes the loop before the audience files out.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3007

Foxe's Acts and Monuments (1563) does cover Oldcastle as a Lollard Protestant martyr; his execution date of 14 December 1417 is confirmed by historical record; The Famous Victories of Henry the Fifth (c. 1586) featuring an Oldcastle character is confirmed; the Admiral's Men Oldcastle play (1599) is documented.
The Oldcastle-to-Falstaff name change, the Cobham pressure, Foxe's martyrology, and the textual trace in 'old lad of the castle' are all mainstream scholarly consensus with no interpretive overreach.
